lines.text: Your phone has a 108 megapixel camera. You are told this makes your phone take better photos. But the sensor captures 108 megapixels — and most days you get 12. What happened to the other 96?
The sensor has a tiny pixel. About 0.8 micrometres wide. Smaller pixels collect less light. So to get more light, the camera merges neighbouring pixels.
For the standard 108 megapixel sensor, this is done nine pixels at a time. A 3-by-3 grid of sensor sites is combined into one output pixel.

That gives a 12 megapixel image. The numbers are right, so you nod. But it is worth noting what the number then means: megapixels, strictly speaking, is a measure of sensor sites — not the pixels the phone actually delivers.
And if you push to full resolution, you are dealing with another cost. Diffraction — light bending around a small lens — starts to blur neighbouring sensor sites together.
Whether this matters for your photos is worth asking rather than assuming. That is exactly the kind of thing to test — at fixed aperture, compare sharpness at the smallest versus largest sensor size.
